title: Phosphorus availability overrides evolutionary adaptation to warming and high carbon dioxide in shaping diatom physiology and lipid metabolism
content:
Abstract

Rising ocean temperatures and CO2 concentrations are reshaping phytoplankton physiology, yet how long-term adaptation to these stressors interacts with nutrient limitation remains poorly understood. Phosphorus (P) frequently limits phytoplankton growth in coastal and stratified oceans, but it remains unclear whether adaptation to warming and elevated CO2 modifies responses to P limitation and whether such adaptive advantages can be realized under nutrient stress. Here, we combined multi-year experimental evolution of the model diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum under warming, elevated CO2, and their combination with short-term assays across a phosphorus gradient to examine how evolutionary history influences responses to P availability. Across all adaptation regimes, P availability overwhelmingly governed growth, photosynthetic performance, and lipidome structure. Long-term adaptation increased maximum growth rate and phosphate affinity, but these advantages were largely suppressed under P limitation. Lipidomic analyses revealed extensive P-driven membrane remodeling, characterized by declines in phospholipids and increases in glycolipids and neutral lipids. While lipid-class remodeling remained highly conserved across adaptation regimes, structural lipid traits responded differently depending on both evolutionary history and phosphorus status. Under P-replete conditions, warming and elevated CO2 primarily promoted fatty-acid elongation, whereas under P limitation they increased fatty-acid desaturation. These results demonstrate that nutrient regimes constrain evolutionary responses to warming and elevated CO2, highlighting phosphorus as a key determinant of diatom resilience in future oceans. Increasing nutrient limitation in future oceans may therefore restrict the extent to which phytoplankton populations can realize adaptive advantages under climate change, with implications for marine productivity and biogeochemical cycling.
